title: Given a board of 'X' and 'O', capture all regions surrounded by 'X' by flipping every 'O' that is not connected to a border 'O' into 'X'. Border-connected 'O's are safe and stay.
shortTitle: Surrounded Regions — mark border-connected 'O's via DFS, flip the rest

s1_definition.profdef: Surrounded Regions inverts the condition: instead of finding surrounded O's directly, it marks every O reachable from a border O as safe via DFS or BFS seeded from the edges, then sweeps the board flipping all unmarked O's to X and restoring the marked ones. Only O's with no escape to the border get captured.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of a compliance grid where an open flag is safe only if it connects to the edge of the jurisdiction. You start from the border open flags and mark everything connected to them as protected. Any open flag that is not protected is fully enclosed by closed cells, so it gets converted to closed. The ones touching the border stay open.
s1_definition.oneliner: Seed DFS/BFS from border O's to mark safe cells, then flip every unmarked O to X and un-mark the safe ones.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Surrounded Regions inverts the condition: instead of finding surrounded O's directly, it marks every O reachable from a border O as safe via DFS or BFS seeded from the edges, then sweeps the board flipping all unmarked O's to X and restoring the marked ones. Only O's with no escape to the border get captured.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of a compliance grid where an open flag is safe only if it connects to the edge of the jurisdiction. You start from the border open flags and mark everything connected to them as protected. Any open flag that is not protected is fully enclosed by closed cells, so it gets converted to closed. The ones touching the border stay open.

**One line to remember:** Seed DFS/BFS from border O's to mark safe cells, then flip every unmarked O to X and un-mark the safe ones.

sections.s2_technical:
Run a search from every O on the four borders, marking each reachable O with a temporary sentinel so it is remembered as safe. For example: start DFS from border cells, marking `board[r][c] = 'S';` for safe.

The search spreads only through O cells, so it marks exactly the O's connected to the border, leaving fully enclosed O's untouched. For example: `if (board[r][c] != 'O') return; board[r][c] = 'S'; recurse four neighbors;`.

After marking, sweep the whole board: any cell still holding O is enclosed and becomes X, while any cell holding the sentinel is safe and is restored to O. For example: `board[r][c] = (board[r][c] == 'S') ? 'O' : 'X';`.

The time is linear in the number of cells, since the border search and the final sweep each touch every cell a constant number of times, and the space is the recursion or queue bounded by the board. A senior nuance is the inversion of the problem: directly detecting surrounded regions is awkward because any single border escape saves a whole region, so marking from the borders outward and capturing the complement is far cleaner, using a temporary sentinel rather than a separate visited matrix to save space.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At National Bank of India, a jurisdiction grid marks open exposures, and an exposure is contained only if it is fully enclosed by closed cells with no path to the border. The system must convert all contained exposures to closed. This is exactly how Surrounded Regions works — flip the enclosed ones, keep the border-connected ones.

Problem 2 — Detecting enclosure directly is error-prone because one border escape protects an entire connected region. This is exactly why the border-seeded marking with complement capture is used.

The mini-project builds an `ExposureContainment` service using border DFS, a `BankLogFormatter`, and a runnable demo over an exposure board.

sections.s5_journey:
The input is a four-by-four board with an enclosed group of open cells in the middle and one open cell on the bottom border.

Step 1: The border scan starts the mark from every edge cell. The bottom-left open cell at three-one is on the border, so it is marked safe.

Step 2: The mark from three-one spreads through connected open cells, but its only open neighbor paths are blocked by closed cells, so just that border cell is marked safe.

Step 3: The middle open group at one-one, one-two, two-two is not reached by any border search because it is fully enclosed by closed cells.

Step 4: The sweep now flips every remaining open cell to closed, converting the enclosed middle group to closed.

Step 5: The sweep restores the sentinel-marked safe cell at three-one back to open.

Step 6: The result keeps the border-connected open cell and captures the enclosed group, exactly as containment requires.

sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  board:                 after containment:
    X X X X                X X X X
    X O O X     ──►        X X X X   (middle O-region enclosed → flipped)
    X X O X                X X X X
    X O X X                X O X X   (bottom-left O on border → safe, stays)

  Step1: DFS from border O's → mark 'S' (safe)
  Step2: remaining 'O' → 'X' (captured);  'S' → 'O' (restored)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Surrounded Regions asks me to flip every O that is fully enclosed by X into X, while leaving any O connected to the border alone. Detecting enclosure directly is awkward, because a single escape to the border protects an entire connected region. So I invert the problem: I mark every O that is reachable from a border O as safe, then capture the complement.

I seed a depth-first or breadth-first search from every O on the four edges, spreading only through O cells and marking each reachable one with a temporary sentinel. That marks exactly the border-connected O's, leaving fully enclosed O's untouched. Then I sweep the board once: any cell still holding O is enclosed and becomes X, and any cell holding the sentinel is restored to O. Using a sentinel instead of a separate visited matrix saves space.

The insight interviewers test is recognizing that marking safe cells from the border and capturing everything else is far cleaner than trying to prove enclosure region by region. The cost is linear in the number of cells, because the border search and the final sweep each touch every cell a constant number of times.

In my project at National Bank of India, a jurisdiction grid marked open exposures, and an exposure counted as contained only if it was fully enclosed with no path to the border. I used the border-seeded marking to protect every exposure connected to an edge, then flipped the rest to closed, which captured exactly the contained exposures and correctly spared any region with even a single border escape.
